papers.title: RAS pathway mutations orchestrate chromatin reconfiguration and transcriptional rewiring in colorectal cancer
papers.authors: Gao Z, Kundu S, Xing P, Davila E, Polavarapu V, Akcan E
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: RAS pathway mutations occur in ~ 40% of colorectal cancers (CRCs), with KRAS- and BRAF- mutant tumors exhibiting distinct mutational, transcriptional, and epigenetic landscapes. Advances in next-generation sequencing enable integrated analyses of multi-omics data, providing insight into their regulatory relationships. To define the molecular programs driven by RAS pathway mutations, we generated isogenic CRC cell models and profiled chromatin accessibility using ATAC-seq.
METHODS: We performed ATAC-seq in isogenic HCT116 and RKO models. Mutation-associated changes in genes, regulatory elements, and signaling pathways were identified, together with inferred transcription factor (TF) binding activity. Clinical datasets were analyzed to assess whether features identified in the cell models were recapitulated in patient tumors and whether they were associated with clinical outcomes.
RESULTS: Isogenic CRC models segregated by RAS pathway mutation status at both epigenetic and transcriptomic levels. Mutation alterations modulated WNT signaling, accompanied by changes in RUNX2 and TCF7L2 expression and binding activity. Comparison between the HCT116 and RKO models identified 85 genes, eight of which displayed reproducible expression patterns across three independent clinical cohorts. TCF7L2 were associated with RAS pathway mutations in patient tumors, with elevated expression level predicting worse overall survival independent of cofactors.
CONCLUSION: We identified RAS pathway mutation-driven regulatory reprogramming with convergent effects on WNT signaling. TCF7L2 emerged as a key TF, with elevated expression in BRAF-mutant tumors independently associated with poor clinical outcomes. These findings highlight a clinically relevant epigenetic mechanism linking RAS pathway mutations to CRC cell survival maintenance.

papers.title: Gut microbiota in genetic diseases: from Mendelian disorders to complex traits
papers.authors: Chen G, Li J, Huang T, Zeng D, Mo L, Li J
papers.abstract: As a core component of the human microecosystem, the dynamic balance of the composition and function of gut microbiota is essential to host health. In recent years, numerous studies have demonstrated that gut dysbiosis is not only associated with metabolic diseases and immune disorders but also plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of hereditary diseases. Ranging from chromosomal diseases (e.g., Down syndrome), monogenic diseases (e.g., cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary hemolytic anemia), mitochondrial diseases (e.g., Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy) to polygenic hereditary diseases (e.g., inflammatory bowel disease, autism spectrum disorder, obesity and diabetes), gut microbiota can markedly alter the manifestation and severity of disease phenotypes by regulating host immune responses, metabolic pathways and gene expression. Nevertheless, the bidirectional interaction network between host genes and gut microbiota has not been fully elucidated. Most existing studies merely focus on correlation analysis, and in-depth exploration of causal mechanisms remains insufficient. This review elaborates on the mechanisms of gut microbiota in monogenic diseases and hereditary diseases with complex phenotypes. By integrating the latest advances in genomics, metabolomics and microbiomics, it discusses how gut dysbiosis affects disease progression via immune modulation, metabolite reprogramming and epigenetic modification. Meanwhile, this paper summarizes the current status and challenges of clinical translation of microbiota-targeted therapies, such as probiotics and fecal microbiota transplantation(FMT), in the treatment of hereditary diseases. This review aims to provide a microecological perspective for understanding the pathogenesis of hereditary diseases and offer theoretical support for personalized and precise intervention.
